chapter.name: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
chapter.blurb: The chapter studies liquids and gases as fluids: the pressure in a fluid at rest, Pascal's law, the increase of pressure with depth, and the barometer, manometer and hydraulic machines built on these ideas. It then treats fluids in motion through streamline flow, the equation of continuity and Bernoulli's principle with its applications to the speed of efflux and dynamic lift. Finally it introduces viscosity with Stokes' law and terminal velocity, and surface tension with the angle of contact, drops and bubbles, and capillary rise.

scope_in.item: State what distinguishes fluids from solids (ability to flow, no definite shape, very small resistance to shear stress) and liquids from gases (fixed volume, compressibility)

Define pressure as normal force per unit area, explain why the force of a fluid at rest on a surface is normal and why pressure is a scalar, give its dimensions and SI unit (Pa) and use 1 atm = 1.01 x 10^5 Pa; calculate pressure from force and area
Define density and relative density, give their dimensions and units, and use them in calculations

State Pascal's law (pressure the same at the same height and in all directions in a fluid at rest; applied pressure transmitted undiminished) and follow its proof with a prism-shaped and a bar-shaped fluid element
Explain the hydraulic lift and hydraulic brakes and calculate forces, mechanical advantage A2/A1 and piston displacements (L1 A1 = L2 A2)
Use P2 - P1 = rho g h and P = Pa + rho g h to find absolute and gauge pressure at a depth; explain the hydrostatic paradox

Describe atmospheric pressure, the mercury barometer (Pa = rho g h, about 76 cm of mercury), the units torr and bar, and the open-tube manometer; solve U-tube problems using equal pressure at equal level
Define steady flow and streamline, explain why streamlines do not cross, distinguish laminar and turbulent flow, and note that flow becomes turbulent beyond a critical speed
State and apply the equation of continuity A v = constant for an incompressible fluid as conservation of mass, including volume flow rate

State Bernoulli's equation P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline, outline its derivation from the work-energy theorem, state its restrictions (steady, non-viscous, incompressible flow) and apply it between two named points
Derive and use the speed of efflux, v = sqrt(2 g h + 2(P - Pa)/rho), and Torricelli's law v = sqrt(2 g h) for an open tank
Explain dynamic lift on a spinning ball (Magnus effect) and on an aerofoil, and estimate lift from the pressure difference (rho/2)(v2^2 - v1^2) times the wing area

Describe viscosity as internal friction between layers, define the coefficient of viscosity eta = (F/A)/(v/l), give its units and dimensions and its variation with temperature for liquids and gases, and calculate eta for a film between plates
State Stokes' law F = 6 pi eta a v and use the terminal velocity v_t = 2 a^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta) of a sphere falling through a fluid

Explain surface energy and surface tension from molecular attraction; use S = F/(2 l) for a film on a slider, S = m g/(2 l) for the plate method and energy = S x area; state that surface tension falls with temperature
Define angle of contact, use S_la cos theta + S_sl = S_sa, and relate acute and obtuse angles of contact to wetting and non-wetting, including the action of wetting and water-proofing agents
Explain why drops and bubbles are spherical and calculate the excess pressure 2 S/r for a liquid drop or an air bubble inside a liquid and 4 S/r for a soap bubble in air
Explain capillary rise and use h = 2 S cos theta/(rho g a), including the fall of mercury in a glass capillary

concepts.name: Fluids, pressure and density
concepts.description: What distinguishes fluids from solids, the definition of pressure as normal force per unit area and why it is a scalar, its unit and dimensions, and density and relative density.
concepts.idea: Liquids and gases can flow because they offer very little resistance to shear stress; what a fluid at rest does to any surface is described by its pressure, the normal force per unit area, and how much matter it packs into a volume is described by its density.
concepts.rule: A fluid has no definite shape of its own; solids and liquids have a fixed volume while a gas fills its container, and solids and liquids are far less compressible than gases. A fluid at rest exerts a force that is always normal to any surface in contact with it. Average pressure P_av = F/A, where F is the magnitude of the normal force on area A. Pressure is a scalar; its dimensions are [M L^-1 T^-2] and its SI unit is N/m^2, named the pascal (Pa); 1 atm = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa (1.01 x 10^5 Pa in the Summary). Density rho = m/V, dimensions [M L^-3], SI unit kg/m^3; a liquid is largely incompressible so its density is nearly constant, while the density of a gas varies greatly with pressure. Relative density = density of the substance / density of water at 4 degrees C (1.0 x 10^3 kg/m^3); it is a dimensionless positive scalar.
concepts.example: A normal force of 50 N spread uniformly over 0.25 m^2 gives P = F/A = 50/0.25 = 200 Pa. A liquid of relative density 0.9 has density 0.9 x 1.0 x 10^3 = 900 kg/m^3.

concepts.name: Pascal's law and hydraulic machines
concepts.description: Pascal's law in both its forms (pressure the same at the same height and in all directions; applied pressure transmitted undiminished) and its use in the hydraulic lift and hydraulic brakes.
concepts.idea: In a fluid at rest the pressure at a point does not depend on direction, and any extra pressure applied to an enclosed fluid shows up everywhere in it; a small force on a small piston can therefore hold a large force on a large piston.
concepts.rule: Pascal's law: the pressure in a fluid at rest is the same at all points at the same height, and it is the same in all directions. Its other form: whenever external pressure is applied on any part of a fluid contained in a vessel, it is transmitted undiminished and equally in all directions. Hydraulic lift: a force F1 on a small piston of area A1 produces pressure P = F1/A1, which is transmitted to a larger piston of area A2, giving F2 = P A2 = F1 A2/A1. The factor A2/A1 is the mechanical advantage. For an incompressible liquid the volume pushed in equals the volume pushed out, L1 A1 = L2 A2. Hydraulic brakes work on the same principle, and the pressure is transmitted equally to all wheel cylinders. Atmospheric pressure is common to both pistons and is ignored.
concepts.example: A force F1 = 20 N on a piston of area 2 cm^2 gives, on a piston of area 50 cm^2 at the same level, F2 = F1 A2/A1 = 20 x 50/2 = 500 N.

concepts.name: Variation of pressure with depth; atmospheric and gauge pressure
concepts.description: The pressure difference rho g h between two levels of a fluid at rest, absolute and gauge pressure, the hydrostatic paradox, the mercury barometer, the units torr and bar, and the open-tube manometer.
concepts.idea: A liquid at rest presses harder the deeper you go, by an amount that depends only on the depth, the density and g, not on the shape or width of the vessel; the atmosphere itself is such a column, and barometers and manometers measure pressure by the height of a liquid column.
concepts.rule: For two points in a fluid at rest separated by a vertical distance h, the lower point 2 is at the higher pressure: P2 - P1 = rho g h. Below the surface of a liquid open to the atmosphere, the absolute pressure at depth h is P = Pa + rho g h; the excess P - Pa = rho g h is the gauge pressure. The pressure depends on the height of the column and not on the cross-sectional area or the shape of the container (hydrostatic paradox), and is the same at all points at the same horizontal level. The pressure of the atmosphere at a point equals the weight of a column of air of unit cross-sectional area extending from that point to the top of the atmosphere. Mercury barometer: Pa = rho g h, with h about 76 cm of mercury at sea level. 1 torr = pressure of 1 mm of mercury = 133 Pa; 1 bar = 10^5 Pa. An open-tube manometer (a U-tube with one end open to the atmosphere) measures gauge pressure, which is proportional to the difference h in the liquid levels.
concepts.example: At a depth of 5 m in fresh water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2, Pa = 1.01 x 10^5 Pa): gauge pressure = rho g h = 1000 x 10 x 5 = 5.0 x 10^4 Pa; absolute pressure = 1.01 x 10^5 + 0.50 x 10^5 = 1.51 x 10^5 Pa.

concepts.name: Streamline flow and the equation of continuity
concepts.description: Steady flow, streamlines and why they never cross, the equation of continuity A v = constant for an incompressible fluid, and the change to turbulent flow beyond a critical speed.
concepts.idea: In steady flow every particle passing a given point does exactly what the previous one did, so the flow can be mapped by fixed streamlines; since an incompressible fluid cannot pile up anywhere, it must move faster where the pipe is narrower.
concepts.rule: The flow is steady if, at any given point, the velocity of each passing fluid particle remains constant in time (the velocity may differ from point to point). A streamline is a curve whose tangent at any point is in the direction of the fluid velocity at that point; it is the path of a particle in steady flow. No two streamlines can cross. Mass crossing each section in the same time is equal: rho_P A_P v_P = rho_R A_R v_R; for an incompressible fluid this becomes the equation of continuity A v = constant, a statement of conservation of mass. A v is the volume flux or flow rate (m^3/s). Where the pipe is narrower the streamlines are closer together and the speed is greater. Steady flow is achieved at low flow speeds; beyond a limiting value called the critical speed the flow becomes turbulent. In laminar flow the velocities at different points may differ in magnitude but their directions are parallel.
concepts.example: Water enters a section of area 6 cm^2 at 2 m/s and leaves through a section of area 3 cm^2. From A1 v1 = A2 v2, v2 = 6 x 2/3 = 4 m/s.

concepts.name: Bernoulli's principle
concepts.description: Bernoulli's equation P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline, how it follows from the work-energy theorem, the conditions under which it holds, and its use between two named points of a flow.
concepts.idea: Bernoulli's equation is energy conservation for a steadily flowing ideal fluid: the work done by pressure forces on a portion of fluid goes into changing its kinetic energy and its gravitational potential energy, so where the fluid speeds up or rises its pressure falls.
concepts.rule: For steady flow of an incompressible, non-viscous fluid, between any two points 1 and 2 along a streamline: P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 + rho g h1 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2 + rho g h2, i.e. P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant. (1/2) rho v^2 is the kinetic energy per unit volume and rho g h the potential energy per unit volume. It follows from the work-energy theorem: (P1 - P2) Delta V = (1/2) rho Delta V (v2^2 - v1^2) + rho g Delta V (h2 - h1). Restrictions: no energy lost to viscosity (real fluids lose some kinetic energy as heat, so the equation is only approximately true), the fluid must be incompressible, and the flow must be steady - it does not hold for non-steady or turbulent flow. For a fluid at rest it reduces to P1 - P2 = rho g (h2 - h1).
concepts.example: Water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3) flows steadily in a horizontal pipe, at 1 m/s at a wide point and 3 m/s at a narrow point. P_wide - P_narrow = (1/2) rho (v2^2 - v1^2) = 0.5 x 1000 x (9 - 1) = 4000 Pa.

concepts.name: Speed of efflux (Torricelli's law) and dynamic lift
concepts.description: The two applications of Bernoulli's principle kept in this edition: the speed of efflux from a tank (Torricelli's law) and dynamic lift on a spinning ball (Magnus effect) and on an aerofoil.
concepts.idea: Applied to a tank with a small hole, Bernoulli's equation says the liquid leaves as fast as if it had fallen freely from the surface; applied to air streaming past a spinning ball or a wing, it says the faster air on one side has the lower pressure, producing a net force called dynamic lift.
concepts.rule: Speed of efflux from a small hole at depth h below the liquid surface in a wide tank whose air space is at pressure P: v1 = sqrt(2 g h + 2 (P - Pa)/rho). The surface is taken to be at rest because the tank's area is much larger than the hole's. If the tank is open to the atmosphere (P = Pa), v1 = sqrt(2 g h), Torricelli's law, the same as the speed of a freely falling body. If P >> Pa, the speed is set by the container pressure (as in rocket propulsion). Dynamic lift is the force on a body (aeroplane wing, hydrofoil, spinning ball) by virtue of its motion through a fluid. A non-spinning ball has symmetrical streamlines and no lift. A spinning ball drags air round with it, so the air speed relative to the ball is larger on one side; the pressure is lower there and a net force acts (Magnus effect). For an aerofoil the streamlines crowd above the wing, the speed is higher and the pressure lower above, giving an upward lift = (pressure difference) x (wing area), with pressure difference = (rho/2)(v2^2 - v1^2) when the small height difference is ignored.
concepts.example: A wide open tank has a small hole 0.45 m below the water surface. With g = 10 m/s^2, v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.45) = sqrt(9) = 3 m/s.

concepts.name: Viscosity, Stokes' law and terminal velocity
concepts.description: Viscosity as internal friction between fluid layers, the coefficient of viscosity as shearing stress divided by strain rate, its units and temperature dependence, Stokes' law for the drag on a sphere and the terminal velocity of a falling sphere.
concepts.idea: Layers of a real fluid moving at different speeds drag on one another; the coefficient of viscosity measures how large a shearing stress is needed for a given rate of shearing, and the same drag brings a small sphere falling through a fluid to a steady terminal velocity.
concepts.rule: Viscosity is the resistance to fluid motion, an internal friction that exists when there is relative motion between layers. The fluid layer in contact with a surface has the velocity of that surface; between a fixed plate and a plate moving with velocity v a distance l away, the layer velocities increase uniformly from zero to v. In a pipe the velocity is greatest along the axis and zero at the walls. Coefficient of viscosity eta = shearing stress/strain rate = (F/A)/(v/l) = F l/(v A). SI unit: poiseuille (Pl) = N s m^-2 = Pa s; dimensions [M L^-1 T^-1]. The viscosity of liquids decreases with temperature while that of gases increases. Stokes' law: the viscous drag on a sphere of radius a moving with velocity v through a fluid of viscosity eta is F = 6 pi eta a v, opposite to the motion. A sphere of density rho falling through a fluid of density sigma reaches terminal velocity when viscous force plus buoyant force equals the force due to gravity: 6 pi eta a v_t = (4 pi/3) a^3 (rho - sigma) g, so v_t = 2 a^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta).
concepts.example: A force of 0.02 N keeps a plate of area 0.5 m^2 moving at 0.1 m/s over a liquid film 1 mm thick. eta = F l/(v A) = (0.02 x 0.001)/(0.1 x 0.5) = 4 x 10^-4 Pa s.

questions.q: You are given two oils of nearly equal density, several identical small steel balls, two tall glass jars, a ruler and a stopwatch. Devise an experiment to decide which oil is more viscous. State what you would measure, how you would use the result, and one precaution that makes the comparison fair.
questions.a: Fill one jar with each oil. Mark two levels on each jar well below the surface, a measured distance apart, so that the ball has reached its constant terminal velocity before the first mark. Drop a ball centrally into each jar and time its fall between the marks; terminal velocity = distance/time. Since v_t = 2 a^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta), with the same ball and nearly the same oil density the terminal velocity is inversely proportional to eta, so the oil in which the ball falls more slowly is the more viscous. Precaution: keep both oils at the same temperature (viscosity changes with temperature), use identical balls, and repeat the timing.
s: Measures the time for a ball to fall a marked distance after it has reached terminal (constant) velocity
Uses v_t inversely proportional to eta: the oil with the smaller terminal velocity is the more viscous
States a valid fairness precaution (same temperature, identical balls, timing only after constant speed is reached, or repeating readings)

concepts.name: Surface energy, surface tension and angle of contact
concepts.description: Why the surface of a liquid has extra energy, surface tension as force per unit length and as surface energy per unit area, the film-and-slider and plate methods of measuring it, and the angle of contact with wetting and non-wetting.
concepts.idea: Molecules at a liquid surface have fewer neighbours and so more energy than those inside; making more surface costs energy, the surface behaves as if under tension, and the way a liquid meets a solid is settled by the balance of the three interfacial tensions.
concepts.rule: A molecule at the surface has roughly half the negative potential energy of one in the bulk, so surface molecules have extra energy and a liquid tends to have the least surface area that conditions permit. For a film held by a sliding bar of length l, moving the bar a distance d increases the area by 2 d l (a film has two surfaces): S (2 d l) = F d, so S = F/(2 l). Surface tension S is the force per unit length acting in the plane of the interface, and equals the surface energy per unit area (N/m = J/m^2). It depends on the materials on both sides of the interface and usually falls with temperature; gases have no free surface and no surface tension. Plate method: S_la = W/(2 l) = m g/(2 l), where W is the extra weight needed to pull a plate of edge length l clear of the liquid. The angle of contact theta is the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface, measured inside the liquid; S_la cos theta + S_sl = S_sa. If theta is obtuse the liquid does not wet the solid (water on a lotus leaf or waxy surface, mercury on glass); if theta is acute it wets the solid (water on glass or plastic). Wetting agents such as soaps and detergents make the angle of contact small; water-proofing agents make it large.
concepts.example: A soap film pulls a slider of length 10 cm with a force of 5.0 x 10^-3 N. S = F/(2 l) = (5.0 x 10^-3)/(2 x 0.10) = 0.025 N/m.

questions.q: The interfacial tensions for a liquid resting on a solid are S_sa = 0.050 N/m (solid-air), S_sl = 0.085 N/m (solid-liquid) and S_la = 0.070 N/m (liquid-air). (a) Using S_la cos theta + S_sl = S_sa, find the angle of contact and say whether the liquid wets the solid. (b) An agent added to the liquid lowers S_sl to 0.015 N/m while the other two values stay the same. Find the new angle of contact and state what has changed.
questions.a: (a) cos theta = (S_sa - S_sl)/S_la = (0.050 - 0.085)/0.070 = -0.50, so theta = 120 degrees. The angle is obtuse, so the liquid does not wet the solid and forms droplets. (b) cos theta = (0.050 - 0.015)/0.070 = +0.50, so theta = 60 degrees. The angle is now acute, so the liquid wets the solid and spreads: the added agent acts as a wetting agent by reducing the solid-liquid interfacial tension.
s: cos theta = -0.50, theta = 120 degrees: obtuse, liquid does not wet the solid
New cos theta = +0.50, theta = 60 degrees
Acute angle: the liquid now wets the solid; the agent lowered S_sl (wetting agent)

questions.q: A film of a liquid on a U-shaped wire with a slider of length 30 cm supports a weight of 4.0 x 10^-2 N. questions.q: A manufacturer wants (i) a fabric for raincoats and (ii) a liquid for washing clothes. Using the idea of angle of contact, propose what kind of agent should be used in each case, describe how water should behave on the fibres in each case, and relate each behaviour to whether the angle of contact is acute or obtuse.
questions.a: (i) Raincoat fabric: treat it with a water-proofing agent, which creates a large (obtuse) angle of contact between water and the fibres. Water then does not wet the fibres; it stays as droplets and runs off. (ii) Washing liquid: add a wetting agent such as soap or detergent, which makes the angle of contact small (acute). The water then wets the fibres, spreads and penetrates well, so the washing is effective. In general an obtuse angle of contact means the liquid does not wet the solid, and an acute angle means it wets and spreads.
s: Raincoat: water-proofing agent giving a large (obtuse) angle of contact, so water forms droplets and does not wet the fibres
Washing liquid: wetting agent (soap/detergent) giving a small (acute) angle of contact, so water spreads and penetrates
States the general link: obtuse angle - non-wetting; acute angle - wetting

concepts.name: Drops, bubbles and capillary rise
concepts.description: Why free drops and bubbles are spherical, the excess pressure inside a liquid drop, an air bubble inside a liquid and a soap bubble in air, and the rise or fall of a liquid in a capillary tube.
concepts.idea: Because a curved liquid surface is under tension, the pressure on its concave side is higher than on its convex side; this excess pressure keeps drops and bubbles in equilibrium and is what pulls water up a narrow tube.
concepts.rule: For a given volume a sphere has the least surface area, so free drops and bubbles are spherical when gravity and other forces are negligible. Excess pressure inside a spherical liquid drop of radius r, or inside an air bubble (cavity) of radius r in a liquid, which has one liquid surface: P_i - P_o = 2 S/r. A soap bubble in air has two liquid-air interfaces: P_i - P_o = 4 S/r. For any liquid-gas interface the concave side has the higher pressure. Capillary rise: water in a narrow glass tube of radius a has a concave meniscus (acute angle of contact theta); the pressure just under the meniscus is less than atmospheric by (2 S/a) cos theta, and h rho g = (2 S cos theta)/a, so h = 2 S cos theta/(rho g a). The rise is larger for a smaller a. If the meniscus is convex (cos theta negative, as for mercury in glass) the liquid stands lower in the capillary.
concepts.example: A liquid drop of radius 0.20 mm with surface tension 0.060 N/m has excess pressure 2 S/r = (2 x 0.060)/(0.20 x 10^-3) = 600 Pa.

The surface tension of a soap solution is 0.030 N/m. (a) Find the excess pressure inside a soap bubble in air of radius 4.0 mm. (b) An air bubble inside the liquid, also of radius 4.0 mm, is formed 50 cm below the surface of the soap solution in an open container. Find the excess pressure inside this air bubble and the absolute pressure inside it. (Density of the soap solution = 1.2 x 10^3 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2, atmospheric pressure = 1.01 x 10^5 Pa.)
questions.a: (a) A soap bubble in air has two surfaces: excess pressure = 4 S/r = (4 x 0.030)/(4.0 x 10^-3) = 30 Pa. (b) An air bubble inside the liquid has one surface: excess pressure = 2 S/r = (2 x 0.030)/(4.0 x 10^-3) = 15 Pa. Pressure outside the bubble P_o = Pa + rho g h = 1.01 x 10^5 + 1.2 x 10^3 x 10 x 0.50 = 1.01 x 10^5 + 6.0 x 10^3 = 1.07 x 10^5 Pa. Absolute pressure inside = P_o + 15 Pa = 1.07015 x 10^5 Pa, about 1.07 x 10^5 Pa.
s: Soap bubble in air: 4 S/r = 30 Pa
Air bubble inside the liquid: 2 S/r = 15 Pa
P_o = 1.01 x 10^5 + 6.0 x 10^3 = 1.07 x 10^5 Pa and P_i = P_o + 15 Pa = 1.07 x 10^5 Pa (to 3 significant figures)

questions.q: Two soap bubbles in air are blown from the same soap solution. Bubble X has radius 1.0 cm and bubble Y has radius 2.0 cm. Which bubble has the greater excess pressure inside it, and by what factor? Give your reasoning.
questions.a: For bubbles of the same solution the excess pressure is inversely proportional to the radius (it is proportional to S/r with the same S and the same numerical factor). The smaller bubble X therefore has the greater excess pressure, twice that of Y, since its radius is half as large.
s: Excess pressure is inversely proportional to the radius for the same solution
The smaller bubble X has twice the excess pressure of Y

Take the surface tension of water = 0.070 N/m, density of water = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2 and atmospheric pressure = 1.01 x 10^5 Pa. Find (a) the absolute pressure in the water just outside the bubble, (b) the excess pressure inside the bubble and (c) the absolute pressure of the air needed in the tube.
questions.a: (a) P_o = Pa + rho g h = 1.01 x 10^5 + 1000 x 10 x 0.10 = 1.01 x 10^5 + 1.0 x 10^3 = 1.02 x 10^5 Pa. (b) The bubble is hemispherical, so its radius equals the radius of the tube, r = 0.50 x 10^-3 m. It is a bubble of gas in a liquid with one liquid surface, so the excess pressure = 2 S/r = (2 x 0.070)/(0.50 x 10^-3) = 280 Pa. (c) P_i = P_o + 2 S/r = 1.02 x 10^5 + 280 = 1.0228 x 10^5 Pa.
s: P_o = Pa + rho g h = 1.02 x 10^5 Pa
Takes r = tube radius 0.50 x 10^-3 m (hemispherical bubble) and finds the excess pressure 2 S/r = 280 Pa

questions.q: In a glass capillary tube of radius 0.50 mm a student sees water rise about 3 cm. She predicts that in a glass tube of radius 5.0 mm the water will rise about 30 cm, 'because a wider tube can hold up more water'. Evaluate her prediction.
questions.a: The prediction is wrong. The capillary rise is caused by the pressure difference across the curved meniscus, and it is inversely proportional to the radius of the tube: it is larger for a smaller radius. A tube ten times wider gives one-tenth of the rise, about 0.3 cm, not 30 cm.
s: Judgement: wrong; capillary rise is inversely proportional to the tube radius (larger for a narrower tube)
Ten times the radius gives one-tenth of the rise, about 0.3 cm

questions.q: You need water to rise at least 10 cm in a vertical glass capillary tube. Take the surface tension of water = 0.070 N/m, the angle of contact = 0 degrees (cos theta = 1), density of water = 1000 kg/m^3 and g = 10 m/s^2. Design the tube: find the largest radius that will do, in mm, and state what rise a tube of half that radius would give, with a reason.
questions.a: From h = 2 S cos theta/(rho g a), the radius needed is a = 2 S cos theta/(rho g h). For h = 0.10 m: a = (2 x 0.070 x 1)/(1000 x 10 x 0.10) = 1.4 x 10^-4 m = 0.14 mm. The rise is larger for a smaller radius, so any radius up to 0.14 mm will do. Since h is inversely proportional to a, a tube of half this radius (0.070 mm) gives twice the rise, 20 cm.
s: Rearranges h = 2 S cos theta/(rho g a) for the radius
Largest radius a = 1.4 x 10^-4 m = 0.14 mm
Half the radius gives twice the rise (20 cm) because h is inversely proportional to a
